story-001.text: While some that night dreamed of the fabulous riches of the East, others dreamed that devils were bearing them away into the unknown distances of the ocean, where they must wander until the end of their lives. J. Fenimore Cooper, “Mercedes of Castile”.

story-003.text: Among people possessed of the keenest spiritual sensitivity, Gratien Duplay occupied that restless place where the force of life’s excitements comes close to breaking through into madness. Very frequent among his critical states were those moments when, freely yielding to the impressions that came flooding in upon him, he would suddenly shudder in an alluringly terrible presentiment of an instantaneous illumination, whose meaning would be the revelation of the meaning of everything. Naturally, human reason, with an instinctive convulsion, thrust back such a deluge, and the outburst of nerves gave way to exhaustion; otherwise something vaster than consciousness, founded perhaps upon a Homeric synthesis, must inevitably have shattered the mind, like a village mill set to work by Niagara.

story-004.text: The fundamental tone of Duplay’s life was a sense of musical enchantment that never left him. The best example of this, one that fully explains such a peculiarity of soul, may be found in the cinematograph, whose pictures, as is well known, are accompanied by music. Silent action, coloured by the sounds of fitting melodies, acquires a poetic hue. Moral perspective is lost: heroism and debauchery, benediction and villainy, while producing different impressions upon the eye, yield in their sum only an absorbing spectacle — the feelings are stirred, but stirred aesthetically. Between the action and the orchestra there spreads the invisible shadow of an elegy, and in that shadow the boundaries of facts are drowned, making of them — let us repeat it — an absorbing spectacle. The cause is musical enchantment; the effect is a play of moved feelings, leading through the shadow of an elegy to the joy of heightened contemplation.

story-005.text: Precisely this same attitude towards all that exists — an attitude of musical exaltation — made up the unvarying tone of Duplay’s life. It was as though an invisible orchestra accompanied him, developing endless variations upon a certain fundamental melody, whose sounds, inaccessible to physical hearing, left an impression of the most perfect musical loveliness. By virtue of such a complication of perception, Duplay’s own person, with all that he did, thought and said, seemed visible to him as if from outside — a character in a play without title or end — an object of observation. Even sufferings, in their blackest and most tormenting degree, Duplay bore along that same road of detached impression; he himself was the audience. And the hero of the play — he was immersed in vivid contemplation, coloured by musical emotion.

story-006.text: At the same time, during troubled and strange sleep, which interwove life with an almost tangible world of distinct dreams, he several times heard music from whose very first bars he awoke in a state of half-mad trembling. This music was a revelation of harmony such as had never yet arisen anywhere. Its beauty was terrifying in the supernatural power of its concords, capable, it seemed, of turning hell into azure. The perfection of this divinely exultant music, beyond the grasp of consciousness, was — as Gratien Duplay felt with his whole being — the full embodiment of the shadows of that great enchantment with which he went through life, and which was, presumably, the echo of some radiant primal source.

story-007.text: Yet on waking, Duplay’s memory refused to restore what he had heard. In vain, still full of whirling impressions, would he snatch up pencil and paper in the deceptive rapture of a false seizure of treasure; the sounds, receding, grew pale, flaring up now and then with a tormenting happiness of sound, fell silent, and the stillness of the night jealously arrested their echo — musical enchantment.

story-010.text: Roumier’s researches in the fields of colour photography and hypnosis, two such different departments of inquiring endeavour, having achieved considerable success, had thereby created for the persistent scholar a numerous and ceaselessly growing circle of admirers. For this reason the doorbell was Roumier’s tormentor, and on the day in question he listened in anguish to its twentieth rattle, remarking to his manservant that, unless the visitor showed particular insistence, it would not be amiss to remind him that the doctor’s consulting hour would end in five minutes.

story-011.text: On returning, however, the servant reported that the visitor, a very sickly-looking man, had shown an irritable and stubborn insistence. Roumier laid aside a pale photograph of blossoming morning clouds and crossed to the writing desk where he received his visitors. Having given a sign to admit the stranger, he saw a man of vulgar appearance, of the market-place rogue type, dressed without regard to fashion and of doubtful tidiness; he was short of stature but dreadfully thin, which served him in place of high heels. A dull suffering flickered in his sunken eyes; his forehead was high, but hidden by strands of black hair forgotten by the comb; the nervousness of an educated man and the coarsening of life’s hard school were mingled in that face, which numbered, perhaps, a little over thirty years.

story-012.text: “I am a musician,” he said, after the customary preliminary phrases had been exchanged, “and I beg you most earnestly not to refuse me a great service. The case you see before you in my person can scarcely have presented itself even in the variety of your practice. My name is Gratien Duplay.

story-013.text: “About a year ago, among dreams whose sensations and details have an almost real significance for me, owing to their, so to speak, printed vividness, I caught a motif, an inexpressible melody which has pursued me since then almost every night. This melody passes all bounds of expressing its power and its qualities by the ordinary means of words; hearing it, I am ready to believe in the music of the spheres; there is something inhuman in its majesty, while the beauty of its harmonies immeasurably surpasses all that has ever yet been played by trumpets and strings. It is built according to laws unknown to us. On waking I remember nothing and, clinging in vain to the impression, the one thing left to me on these occasions, like a feather of the firebird, I try to discover the spring whose sweet drop increases tenfold the thirst of one perishing in a waterless land. Perhaps in sleep our soul is more receptive; though I know, though I remember, that I have heard this wondrous music, I am nevertheless powerless to hold in my memory even a single bar. However that may be, I earnestly beg you to apply all your art either to strengthening my memory, or else, if it is possible, to the direct power of suggestion, under whose irresistible pressure I might play, in your presence (I have brought my violin), all that so distinctly stirs me in my sleep. This experiment may yield two consequences of differing importance: the first, that the perfection of the mysterious music will prove to be a dreaming distortion of the senses, as often happens with those who dream that they are reading a book of the highest talent, and yet, on waking, recall only a string of senseless phrases; in that case, convinced of my self-deception, I shall resort to systematic treatment, quite content in the knowledge that I lose but little by it; the second consequence, the fixing of the melody in notes, is immeasurably more important. Perhaps the whole musical world of times past and present will vanish in new discoveries, as seeds vanish on becoming flowers, or as the caterpillar ceases, at the appointed hour, to be a hidden, exultant butterfly. Perhaps the very consciousness of mankind will change, shifted upon its foundations, because, I repeat it, and in this I believe myself, the power of that music has in it something divine and shattering.”

story-014.text: Duplay said all this accompanying his speech with vigorous yet fluent gestures; his manner of speaking revealed a man accustomed to discoursing not only upon banal or domestic matters; his gaze, though strained and betraying an extreme nervousness, was free of any shadow of madness, and Roumier found that the experiment promised, at all events, to be interesting. Before proceeding with it, however, he thought it necessary to warn Duplay of the danger attending so violent a disturbance of the senses in the hypnotic state.

story-015.text: “You,” said Roumier, “probably do not suspect the trap into which you may be lured by an excessive excitation of the brain, should it prove (one must allow for this) powerless to restore what does not exist. Granting that this melody is merely a strikingly clear notion, a desire, a craving, whatever you please, but not the music itself, I may reward you with a grave mental illness: even death threatens you in the event of a cerebral haemorrhage, which is possible.”

story-016.text: “I am ready,” said Duplay. “Kindly have my violin brought in.”

story-017.text: When this had been done, and Duplay, bow and violin in hand, had settled himself in a deep, comfortable armchair, Roumier, in no more than a minute, put him to sleep by gaze and command.

story-018.text: “Gratien Duplay!” said the doctor, feeling an unaccustomed agitation. “I command you to hear me and to obey me in everything without exception.”

story-019.text: “I obey,” Duplay answered in a deathly voice.

story-020.text: Roumier’s apartment was on the ground floor, its windows giving onto a small lane. The study window was open. The musician sat not far from the window. He was motionless and pale; large drops of cold sweat ran down his face. Roumier, after a pause, said:

story-021.text: “Duplay! You hear the music you told me of.”

story-022.text: Duplay trembled; his unseeing eyes opened wide and wild, and a lightning-flash of ecstasy transformed his face, like a sea, dull until then, that has suddenly begun to sparkle in the sun. A long moan, like the dying hum of a bell, filled the room.

story-024.text: “Now,” trembling himself in the flood of that nervous radiation invisibly diffused by the musician, “now,” Roumier went on, “you are to play what you hear. The violin is in your hands. Begin!”

story-025.text: Duplay rose and swept his bow sharply, and the hypnotist’s heart, under the force of a sudden rush of blood, began to pound painfully. At the very first sounds that flew from the strings of Duplay’s violin, Roumier understood that he must not listen any further. Those sounds blinded and cast one down. No one could have put them into words. Roumier only felt that his whole life, such as it had passed up to that day, was utterly needless to him, hateful and useless, and that under the spell of such music a man, whoever he might be, would accomplish anything with the same fury of rapture: the greatest crime and the greatest sacrifice. An anguished dread took hold of him; with an effort almost superhuman in that state, Roumier tore the violin from Duplay’s hands, feeling as though he had spat in the face of a god, and, having thus broken the annihilating enchantment, cried:

story-026.text: “Duplay! You heard nothing and played nothing. You have entirely forgotten all that took place during your sleep. Sit down and wake!”

story-027.text: Duplay sat down and drowsily opened his eyes. His awakening left him with a feeling of boundless anguish; he remembered only why he had come to Roumier, and, having recalled this, asked the question that followed from it.

story-028.text: “That was to be expected,” said Roumier, standing with his back to him and turning round only after he had mastered his agitation. “You played a few operetta airs, mixed up with scraps of Schubert’s Serenade.”

story-029.text: After the brief conversation that followed Roumier’s words, Duplay, apologising in confusion, thanked him and went out into the street. There, within his first few steps, a stranger, decently dressed, overtook and stopped him; the man was extremely agitated; glancing at Duplay’s violin and bowing hastily, he asked:

story-030.text: “Forgive me, was it not you who was playing just now behind the window that looks onto the lane? Your music broke off suddenly; I happened to be passing there, I heard it, and I should like to hear it again. What were you playing?! My question is not an idle one: I, a former officer, sobbed like a little child, amid the noise and bustle of the day, from feelings I had never known. What is it, for God’s sake, and who are you?”

story-031.text: Duplay, who had begun to listen absently, grasped the truth in an instant as the passer-by finished speaking. Fury seized him. Leaving the man with a haste both insulting and alarming, he rushed back, rang, and in less than a minute was again standing before the astonished hypnotist. Rage had robbed him of all coherence of speech; choking, he cried:

story-032.text: “You hid it!… Hid it!… Scoundrel! Do you know what you have taken from me?! Worse than murder! There is no forgiveness! Death!… Death for this!”

story-033.text: He threw himself upon Roumier and bore him to the floor, raining blows on him. At that moment the servants appeared, drawn by the noise. Not without difficulty they bound Duplay, who afterwards, on the doctor’s orders, was taken to the asylum.

story-034.text: From then on he lived there, showing every sign of incurable melancholia, broken from time to time by fits of the most unbridled frenzy. In his quiet spells he would play his violin for hours on end, with anguish and tears, searching for what he had lost and astonishing the doctors with the originality of certain fantasias, which he composed ceaselessly. Sometimes, amid variations on one particularly mournful theme, strange bars flew from beneath his bow that made the listeners turn pale: flashes of an exhausted beauty, hints of something greater… but this happened ever more rarely, and it ended with his death, which came in a delirium full of ardent pleas to raise the pitiless curtain that hid a mysterious and beautiful spectacle.
